claim: Translational readthrough gives rise to low abundance proteins with C-terminal extensions beyond the stop codon.
source: Translational readthrough gives rise to low abundance proteins with C-terminal extensions beyond the stop codon.
evidence: This is a general statement about translational readthrough that is supported by established scientific knowledge and is referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: A new regression model was developed to estimate the readthrough propensity (RTP) of all stop codon contexts of the human genome in silico.
source: To identify functional translational readthrough, we estimated the readthrough propensity (RTP) of all stop codon contexts of the human genome by a new regression model in silico
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of this computational model in the Methods and Results sections.

claim: A nucleotide consensus motif for high RTP was identified using the regression model.
source: identified a nucleotide consensus motif for high RTP by using this model
evidence: The consensus motif UGA CUA is derived from the regression model and validated experimentally.

claim: All readthrough extensions were analyzed in silico with a new predictor for peroxisomal targeting signal type 1 (PTS1).
source: analyzed all readthrough extensions in silico with a new predictor for peroxisomal targeting signal type 1 (PTS1)
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of a PTS1 prediction algorithm adapted for human proteins.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase B (LDHB) showed the highest combined RTP and PTS1 probability.
source: Lactate dehydrogenase B (LDHB) showed the highest combined RTP and PTS1 probability.
evidence: This is supported by the computational analysis and confirmed in Figure 3A showing LDHB at position 1 of 42,069 entries.

claim: At least 1.6% of the total cellular LDHB is targeted to the peroxisome by a conserved hidden PTS1.
source: Experimentally we show that at least 1.6% of the total cellular LDHB is targeted to the peroxisome by a conserved hidden PTS1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dual reporter assays showing 1.55-1.6% readthrough and immunofluorescence microscopy showing peroxisomal localization.

claim: The readthrough-extended lactate dehydrogenase subunit LDHBx can co-import LDHA into peroxisomes.
source: The readthrough-extended lactate dehydrogenase subunit LDHBx can also co-import LDHA, the other LDH subunit, into peroxisomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally by co-expression experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: Peroxisomal LDH is conserved in mammals.
source: Peroxisomal LDH is conserved in mammals
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 9 demonstrating conservation of the PTS1 extension exclusively in mammals.

claim: Peroxisomal LDH likely contributes to redox equivalent regeneration in peroxisomes.
source: Peroxisomal LDH is conserved in mammals and likely contributes to redox equivalent regeneration in peroxisomes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the known function of LDH and the metabolic requirements of peroxisomes.

claim: When a stop codon enters the ribosomal A site, release factors bind the stop codon, hydrolyze the peptidyl-tRNA bond, and trigger the release of the polypeptide from the ribosome.
source: When a stop codon enters the ribosomal A site, release factors bind the stop codon, hydrolyze the peptidyl-tRNA bond, and trigger the release of the polypeptide from the ribosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of translation termination.

claim: If a near-cognate aminoacyl-tRNA pairs with the stop codon in the ribosomal A site instead of release factor 1 (eRF1), the stop signal is suppressed.
source: If instead of release factor 1 (eRF1), a near-cognate aminoacyl-tRNA pairs with the stop codon in the ribosomal A site, the stop signal is suppressed.
evidence: This describes the molecular mechanism of translational readthrough, which is established knowledge.

claim: Decoding of a stop codon as a sense codon is known as translational readthrough.
source: Such decoding of a stop codon as a sense codon is known as translational readthrough.
evidence: This is a definition supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: Translational readthrough results in the synthesis of C-terminally extended proteins.
source: As a consequence, translation continues to the next stop codon resulting in the synthesis of C-terminally extended proteins (Baranov et al., 2002; Namy et al., 2004; Firth and Brierley, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Termination occurs with less than 100% efficiency in normal physiology.
source: Mutant tRNAs are classic stop codon suppressors, but termination also occurs with less than 100% efficiency in normal physiology.
evidence: This is established knowledge about translation termination.

claim: A number of cis-elements on the mRNA, typically 3′ of the stop codon together with trans-acting factors, are known to influence stop codon readthrough.
source: A number of cis-elements on the mRNA, typically 3′ of the stop codon together with trans-acting factors, are known to influence stop codon readthrough (Firth et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A case of translational readthrough dependent on RNA cis-elements has recently been found and termed programmed translational readthrough (PTR).
source: A case of translational readthrough dependent on RNA cis-elements has recently been found and termed programmed translational readthrough (PTR) (Eswarappa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: The stop codon itself and the nucleotides before and after the stop codon affect readthrough.
source: But it is also known that the stop codon itself and the nucleotides before and after the stop codon affect readthrough.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the subsequent discussion and citations.

claim: The three stop codons differ in their tendency to be suppressed.
source: The three stop codons differ in their tendency to be suppressed.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by subsequent specific claims about individual stop codons.

claim: In human, UAA is least and UGA is most likely to allow readthrough.
source: In human, UAA is least and UGA is most likely to allow readthrough (Beier and Grimm, 2001; Baranov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The nucleotide immediately downstream of the stop codon is biased and can strongly influence readthrough.
source: Studies also show that the nucleotide immediately downstream of the stop codon is biased and can strongly influence readthrough (McCaughan et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Basal translational readthrough (BTR) is translational readthrough that is entirely dependent on the stop codon and the nucleotides in its immediate vicinity.
source: We here define translational readthrough that is entirely dependent on the stop codon and the nucleotides in its immediate vicinity as basal translational readthrough (BTR).
evidence: This is a definition introduced by the authors in this manuscript.

claim: BTR is independent of cis-acting elements and differs from pharmacologically induced readthrough.
source: Thus BTR is independent of cis-acting elements and also differs from pharmacologically induced readthrough.
evidence: This is part of the definition of BTR introduced by the authors.

claim: Induction of readthrough by aminoglycoside antibiotics is an attractive strategy in the treatment of genetic disorders caused by premature stop codons.
source: Induction of readthrough, most prominently by aminoglycoside antibiotics, is an attractive strategy in the treatment of the large number of genetic disorders caused by premature stop codons (Bidou et al., 2012; Keeling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In viruses, readthrough optimizes the coding capacity of compact genomes.
source: In viruses, readthrough optimizes the coding capacity of compact genomes (Firth and Brierley, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the eukaryotic release factor eRF3 can form prion-like polymers, which introduces a level of epigenetic regulation not found in other eukaryotes.
source: In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the eukaryotic release factor eRF3 can form prion-like polymers, which introduces a level of epigenetic regulation not found in other eukaryotes (Tuite and Cox, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In fungi, translational readthrough extends cytosolic glycolytic enzymes by a cryptic peroxisomal targeting signal.
source: In fungi, translational readthrough extends cytosolic glycolytic enzymes by a cryptic peroxisomal targeting signal (Freitag et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In Drosophila, readthrough is known to affect between 200 and 300 proteins.
source: In Drosophila, readthrough is known to affect between 200 and 300 proteins (Jungreis et al., 2011; Dunn et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In mammals readthrough has been described for more than 50 individual transcripts.
source: in mammals readthrough has been described for more than 50 individual transcripts (Geller and Rich, 1980; Chittum et al., 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 2012; Dunn et al., 2013; Eswarappa et al., 2014; Loughran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ribosome profiling and phylogenetic approaches provide powerful methods for the systematic identification of readthrough in mammals.
source: Ribosome profiling and phylogenetic approaches provide powerful methods for the systematic identification of readthrough in mammals (Jungreis et al., 2011; Dunn et al., 2013; Eswarappa et al., 2014; Loughran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study concentrated on proteins deriving from BTR to find a physiological role for translational readthrough in humans.
source: We wanted to find a physiological role for translational readthrough in humans by identifying C-terminal extensions with targeting signals that would create a functional difference between the normal and the readthrough-extended form. To achieve this aim, we concentrated on proteins deriving from BTR.
evidence: This describes the rationale and approach of the study.

claim: Regression coefficients were assigned to all possible nucleotides in the stop codon context (SCC) based on experimental data.
source: Based on experimental data, we assigned regression coefficients to all possible nucleotides in the stop codon context (SCC)
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used in the study.

claim: The regression coefficients were used to estimate the readthrough propensity (RTP) of all stop codons in the human genome or transcriptome.
source: using those regression coefficients, estimated the readthrough propensity (RTP) of all stop codons in the human genome or transcriptome.
evidence: This describes the application of the computational model.

claim: A new nucleotide consensus for high RTP was formally derived from the regression coefficients of the model.
source: We were able to formally derive a new nucleotide consensus for high RTP from the regression coefficients of our model.
evidence: This describes a key finding of the computational analysis.

claim: All predicted C-terminal extensions were screened for peroxisomal targeting signals.
source: Then we screened all predicted C-terminal extensions for peroxisomal targeting signals
evidence: This describes the screening approach used in the study.

claim: Peroxisomes import most of their matrix proteins through a short targeting signal (PTS1) at the very C-terminus.
source: because peroxisomes import most of their matrix proteins through a short targeting signal (PTS1) at the very C-terminus (Smith and Aitchison, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LDHB combines a very high translational readthrough with a hidden, yet functional and evolutionarily conserved, PTS1.
source: We here show that lactate dehydrogenase B (LDHB) combines a very high translational readthrough with a hidden, yet functional and evolutionarily conserved, PTS1.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The peroxisomal isoform of LDH, containing the readthrough-extended LDHBx subunit, is likely to be involved in the regeneration of redox equivalents for peroxisomal β-oxidation.
source: This peroxisomal isoform of LDH, containing the readthrough-extended LDHBx subunit, is likely to be involved in the regeneration of redox equivalents for peroxisomal β-oxidation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the known function of LDH and peroxisomal metabolism.

claim: The computational method to assess the RTP of all human SCCs focused on SCCs comprising 15 nucleotides including and surrounding the stop codon (nucleotides −6 to +9, stop codon at positions 1 to 3).
source: In order to develop a computational method to assess the RTP of all human SCCs that would allow the identification of genes with high BTR, we focused on SCCs comprising 15 nucleotides including and surrounding the stop codon (nucleotides −6 to +9, stop codon at positions 1 to 3).
evidence: This describes the specific parameters of the computational model.

claim: SCCs were formalized using a binary vector that represented the stop context in a multi-dimensional vector space.
source: we formalized SCCs using a binary vector that represented the stop context in a multi-dimensional vector space (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the computational methodology and is illustrated in figures.

claim: The three stop codons were condensed into one position, so that the binary vector required 51 dimensions.
source: The three stop codons were condensed into one position, so that the binary vector required 51 dimensions, for the four possible nucleotides in the six positions before and after the stop codon, and for the three stop codons (12 × 4 + 3).
evidence: This describes the specific implementation of the computational model.

claim: For the first approximation model (LIN), 66 sequences derived from human nonsense mutations were used.
source: For the first approximation model (LIN), we used 66 sequences derived from human nonsense mutations (Floquet et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data source for the initial model.

claim: The nucleotide sequences of stop contexts from human nonsense mutations show no bias with respect to RTP, because the contexts and the stop codons evolved independently.
source: The nucleotide sequences of these stop contexts show no bias with respect to RTP, because the contexts and the stop codons evolved independently, and therefore the context nucleotides are random in relation to the stop codon.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of the data used.

claim: A linear regression model was calculated for the SCCs using only the experimental BTR values that had been measured in the absence of aminoglycosides.
source: We calculated a linear regression model for these SCCs and used only the experimental BTR values that had been measured in the absence of aminoglycosides.
evidence: This describes the specific methodology used to build the model.

claim: The model assigns regression coefficients to all possible nucleotides in the stop context.
source: The model assigns regression coefficients to all possible nucleotides in the stop context (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the output of the computational model and is illustrated in a figure.

claim: The SCCs for each transcript were extracted from the Ensembl database for genome-wide RTP prediction.
source: For a first round of whole-genome RTP prediction, we extracted the SCCs for each transcript from the Ensembl database
evidence: This describes the data source for genome-wide analysis.

claim: RTP was calculated by adding up the regression coefficients of all relevant positions.
source: calculated RTP by adding up the regression coefficients of all relevant positions.
evidence: This describes the calculation method for RTP.

claim: Candidate transcripts with high, intermediate, and low RTP were selected and tested using a dual reporter assay to expand the data basis of the RTP algorithm.
source: To expand the data basis of the RTP algorithm and to obtain evidence that the algorithm indeed predicts BTR values, we selected candidate transcripts with high, intermediate, and low RTP and tested them using a dual reporter assay (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental validation approach.

claim: SCCs spanning 10 nucleotides upstream and downstream of the stop codon were expressed with a 5′/N-terminal yellow fluorescent protein (Venus) and a 3′/C-terminal humanized Renilla luciferase (hRluc) tag for experimental analysis.
source: For experimental analysis, SCCs spanning 10 nucleotides upstream and downstream of the stop codon were expressed with a 5′/N-terminal yellow fluorescent protein (Venus) and a 3′/C-terminal humanized Renilla luciferase (hRluc) tag.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Stop suppression leads to the expression of hRluc, and Venus served as an internal expression control.
source: Stop suppression leads to the expression of hRluc, and Venus served as an internal expression control.
evidence: This describes the principle of the dual reporter assay.

claim: Readthrough is expressed as luciferase activity per Venus fluorescence.
source: Readthrough is expressed as luciferase activity per Venus fluorescence.
evidence: This describes how readthrough is quantified in the assay.

claim: The dual reporter assay approach excludes introns and exon junction complexes.
source: This approach excludes introns and exon junction complexes
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental design.

claim: The dual reporter assay does not allow for extensive RNA structures that could modulate readthrough due to the relatively short stretch of variable nucleotides between the reporters.
source: due to the relatively short stretch of variable nucleotides between the reporters, also does not allow for extensive RNA structures that could modulate readthrough.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental design.

claim: The dual reporter assay focuses on the assessment of BTR not influenced by specific cis-elements.
source: Consequently, this form of the dual reporter assay focuses on the assessment of BTR not influenced by specific cis-elements.
evidence: This is a conclusion about what the assay measures based on its design.

claim: The additional candidates tested showed BTR between 0.10% (±0.006%) and 2.91% (±0.15%) relative to the 100% readthrough control.
source: The additional candidates tested showed BTR between 0.10% (±0.006%) and 2.91% (±0.15%) relative to the 100% readthrough control expressing the Venus-hRluc fusion protein without an intervening stop codon region (Figure 1C and Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the dual reporter assays.

claim: The aminoglycoside antibiotic geneticin (G418) increased readthrough by between 3.25 (±0.41) and 40.38 (±5.33)-fold.
source: The aminoglycoside antibiotic geneticin (G418) increased readthrough by between 3.25 (±0.41) and 40.38 (±5.33)-fold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the dual reporter assays.

claim: Geneticin could only increase the luciferase-per-Venus signal when a stop codon separated Venus and luciferase, indicating that the dual reporter assay faithfully reports readthrough.
source: Geneticin could only increase the luciferase-per-Venus signal when a stop codon separated Venus and luciferase, indicating that our dual reporter assay faithfully reports readthrough.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data that validates the assay.

claim: The finding that experimental readthrough could be increased by treatment with aminoglycosides excludes alternative mechanisms such as RNA editing or splicing that might explain the relative increase of the luciferase over the Venus signal.
source: The finding that experimental readthrough could be increased by treatment with aminoglycosides also excludes alternative mechanisms such as RNA editing or splicing that might explain the relative increase of the luciferase over the Venus signal.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental results.

claim: The highest levels of induction can only be reached when basal readthrough is low, and a high BTR somewhat limits the maximum induction factor.
source: The highest levels of induction can only be reached when basal readthrough is low, and, vice versa, a high BTR somewhat limits the maximum induction factor (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Maximal BTR readthrough is limited to levels below 15%.
source: suggesting that maximal BTR readthrough is limited to levels below 15%.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on geneticin induction.

claim: The candidate sequences and their experimentally determined readthrough levels were added to obtain an iterative and extended RTP model (LINiter).
source: Next we added our candidate sequences and their experimentally determined readthrough levels to obtain an iterative and extended RTP model (LINiter).
evidence: This describes the refinement of the computational model.

claim: For the LINiter model, a weak but significant Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.34 (p = 0.002) was obtained by leave-one-out cross-validation.
source: For the LINiter model, we obtained a weak but significant Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.34 (p = 0.002) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical measure of the model's performance.

claim: Nucleotide positions associated with coefficients of large absolute value contribute most to RTP.
source: Nucleotide positions associated with coefficients of large absolute value contribute most to RTP.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the linear regression model.

claim: The three or four nucleotides following the stop codon contribute to readthrough.
source: The sequence-logo representation of regression factors in Figure 2A indicates that the three or four nucleotides following the stop codon contribute to readthrough.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of regression coefficients shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The nucleotide positions with the strongest influence on BTR in humans were identified by feature selection.
source: We identified the nucleotide positions with the strongest influence on BTR in humans by feature selection, that is by successively eliminating those positions that contribute least to the prediction (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the computational analysis method.

claim: Two reduced models improve the prediction: LINfs5 and LINfs3.
source: We find that two reduced models improve the prediction. Models with either five or three relevant context positions in addition to the stop codon correspond to the local and global residual error minimum, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the feature selection analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LINfs5 comprises nucleotide position −6, the stop codon, and positions +4 to +7.
source: LINfs5 comprises nucleotide position −6, the stop codon, and positions +4 to +7
evidence: This describes the composition of the LINfs5 model.

claim: LINfs3 comprises only the stop codon and positions +4 to +6, that is the codon following the stop.
source: LINfs3 comprises only the stop codon and positions +4 to +6, that is the codon following the stop (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the composition of the LINfs3 model.

claim: In humans the stop codon and the three nucleotides immediately downstream of the stop codon have the largest influence on BTR.
source: The results of this analysis indicate that in humans the stop codon and the three nucleotides immediately downstream of the stop codon have the largest influence on BTR (LINfs3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the feature selection analysis.

claim: The consensus for high BTR in humans is UGA CUA (stop codon underlined).
source: The corresponding consensus is UGA CUA (stop codon underlined).
evidence: This is derived from the LINfs3 model.

claim: The nucleotides at positions +7 (the fourth position after the stop) and −6 possibly also contribute to BTR.
source: Possibly also the nucleotides at positions +7 (the fourth position after the stop) and −6 contribute to BTR.
evidence: This is suggested by the LINfs5 model.

claim: The RTP-BTR correlation associated with LINfs3 was 0.41 (p = 0.0001).
source: The RTP-BTR correlation associated with LINfs3 was 0.41 (p = 0.0001) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical measure of the LINfs3 model's performance.

claim: Four additional candidate SCCs were analyzed to test if the LINfs3 consensus indeed confers high BTR.
source: To test if the LINfs3 consensus indeed confers high BTR, we analyzed four additional candidate SCCs.
evidence: This describes the experimental validation approach.

claim: Three high-RTP SCCs were derived from AQP4, SYTL2, and CACNA2D4, and DHX38 was used as a control with a low RTP.
source: Three high-RTP SCCs were derived from AQP4, SYTL2, and CACNA2D4, and DHX38 was used as a control with a low RTP.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for validation.

claim: AQP4, SYTL2, and CACNA2D4 conform with the LINfs3 consensus, whereas DHX38 does not.
source: AQP4, SYTL2, and CACNA2D4 conform with the LINfs3 consensus, whereas DHX38 does not.
evidence: This describes the sequence characteristics of the test candidates.

claim: AQP4, SYTL2, and CACNA2D4 showed 2.29% (±0.09%), 0.99% (±0.06%), and 0.61% (±0.02%) readthrough in HeLa cells, whereas for DHX38 readthrough was only 0.27% (±0.04%).
source: AQP4, SYTL2, and CACNA2D4 showed 2.29% (±0.09%), 0.99% (±0.06%), and 0.61% (±0.02%) readthrough in HeLa cells, whereas for DHX38 readthrough was only 0.27% (±0.04%) (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is experimental data from dual reporter assays.

claim: The LINfs3 SCC allows a very high rate of stop suppression.
source: confirming that LINfs3 SCC indeed allows a very high rate of stop suppression.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental validation data.

claim: Dual reporter experiments were performed using the HT1080 fibrosarcoma cell line, the human embryonic kidney cell line (HEK), and the U373 cell line to test if conclusions obtained in HeLa cells can be extended to other cell types.
source: Next we wanted to test if these conclusions obtained in HeLa cells can be extended to other cell types. We therefore performed dual reporter experiments using the HT1080 fibrosarcoma cell line, the human embryonic kidney cell line (HEK), and the U373 cell line.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach to test cell-type specificity.

claim: In all cell types tested, the relative distribution of BTR values remained the same, with AQP4 showing the highest and DHX38 the lowest BTR.
source: In all these experiments, the relative distribution of BTR values remained the same, with AQP4 showing the highest and DHX38 the lowest BTR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from multiple cell types.

claim: The finding that readthrough is lower in CACNA2D4 than in AQP4 and SYTL2 can be taken as evidence that SCC position +7 (fourth after the stop) makes a contribution.
source: The finding that readthrough is lower in CACNA2D4 than in AQP4 and SYTL2 can also be taken as evidence that SCC position +7 (fourth after the stop) makes a contribution.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: BTR is a property of the respective SCC.
source: these experiments show that BTR is indeed a property of the respective SCC
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments in multiple cell types.

claim: Readthrough may be differently regulated in different tissues.
source: readthrough may be differently regulated in different tissues.
evidence: This is suggested by the variation in absolute readthrough levels across cell types.

claim: A partially overlapping set of genes with the UGA CUA consensus was recently tested.
source: A partially overlapping set of genes with this consensus was recently tested (Loughran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Ribosome profiling, phylogenetic approaches, and RTP screening are complementary approaches for identifying translational readthrough.
source: An overview of all experimentally confirmed cases of translational readthrough shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 reveals that ribosome profiling, phylogenetic approaches, and RTP screening are complementary approaches.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing different experimental approaches shown in the Venn diagram.

claim: Only one of the 42 readthrough genes found by ribosome profiling in foreskin fibroblasts contains the UGA CUA consensus.
source: For example, only one of the 42 readthrough genes found by ribosome profiling in foreskin fibroblasts (Dunn et al., 2013) contains the UGA CUA consensus.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing datasets.

claim: The widely varying levels and sequence requirements for efficient stop codon suppression suggest that multiple molecular mechanisms can cause readthrough in mammals.
source: The widely varying levels and sequence requirements for efficient stop codon suppression suggest that multiple molecular mechanisms can cause readthrough in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference from the diversity of readthrough contexts and levels observed.

claim: The extensions were screened for possible transmembrane domains, prenylation sites, endoplasmic retention signals, and glycosylation sites.
source: We have therefore screened the extensions for possible elements that could confer functional differences between the normal and the extended form of the protein. We screened the extensions for possible transmembrane domains (Krogh et al., 2001), for prenylation sites (Zhang and Casey, 1996), for endoplasmic retention signals (Zerangue et al., 2001; Stornaiuolo et al., 2003), and for glycosylation sites (Zielinska et al., 2010; Schwarz and Aebi, 2011).
evidence: This describes the screening approach with citations to methods.

claim: The study focused on the detection of proteins carrying a hidden peroxisomal targeting signal type 1 (PTS1) in the extension to identify genes with a high BTR and a readthrough extension conferring a biological function.
source: To identify genes with a high BTR and a readthrough extension conferring a biological function, we decided to focus on the detection of proteins carrying a hidden peroxisomal targeting signal type 1 (PTS1) in the extension.
evidence: This describes the rationale for focusing on PTS1.

claim: Translational readthrough had been shown to divert a small fraction of cytosolic glycolytic proteins to peroxisomes in fungi.
source: This targeting mechanism had been shown to divert a small fraction of cytosolic glycolytic proteins to peroxisomes in fungi (Freitag et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PTS1 cover more than 90% of the targeting motifs of peroxisomal matrix proteins.
source: PTS1 cover more than 90% of the targeting motifs of peroxisomal matrix proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peroxisomal protein targeting.

claim: The alternative PTS2 is found in only very few matrix proteins, and has even been lost in some organisms.
source: The alternative PTS2 is found in only very few matrix proteins, and has even been lost in some organisms (Lanyon-Hogg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PTS1 is localized at the very C-terminus of a substrate protein.
source: PTS1 is localized at the very C-terminus of a substrate protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTS1.

claim: The quintessential PTS1, Ser-Lys-Leu (SKL), is neither necessary nor sufficient to support matrix protein import into peroxisomes.
source: However, the quintessential PTS1, Ser-Lys-Leu (SKL), is neither necessary nor sufficient to support matrix protein import into peroxisomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTS1 variability.

claim: Variations of PTS1 exist, and amino acids upstream of the terminal tripeptide also contribute to targeting.
source: Variations exist, and amino acids upstream of the terminal tripeptide also contribute to targeting (Brocard and Hartig, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PTS1 does not confer a binary decision (to import or not to import), but is likely to determine an equilibrium between cytosolic and peroxisomal localization.
source: Moreover, PTS1 does not confer a binary decision (to import or not to import), but is likely to determine an equilibrium between cytosolic and peroxisomal localization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTS1 function.

claim: The peroxisomal marker protein catalase has an inherently weak PTS1 which is associated with low affinity to the cytosolic PTS1-receptor PEX5, and a considerable amount of catalase is not imported into peroxisomes.
source: This is best exemplified by the peroxisomal marker protein catalase, a considerable amount of which is not imported into peroxisomes due to an inherently weak PTS1 which is associated with low affinity to the cytosolic PTS1-receptor PEX5 (Maynard et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A PTS1 prediction algorithm previously developed for plants was adapted to human PTS1.
source: We took advantage of these scalable properties of PTS1 and adapted to human PTS1 a prediction algorithm that we had previously developed for plants (Lingner et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the computational methodology with citation.

claim: The machine learning-based PTS1 prediction method has been shown to accurately predict proteins with canonical and non-canonical PTS1 peptides and provides evidence for peroxisome targeting in terms of a posterior probability.
source: This machine learning-based method has been shown to accurately predict proteins with canonical and non-canonical PTS1 peptides and provides evidence for peroxisome targeting in terms of a posterior probability (Lingner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Orthology searches on 24 known human PTS1 sequences in metazoa were conducted using BLAST against protein and EST databases to program the human PTS1 prediction algorithm.
source: To program the human PTS1 prediction algorithm, we conducted orthology searches on 24 known human PTS1 sequences in metazoa using BLAST against protein and EST databases.
evidence: This describes the data collection for the PTS1 prediction algorithm.

claim: The PTS1 posterior probabilities of all predicted C-terminal readthrough extensions derived from the human transcriptome were calculated.
source: We calculated the PTS1 posterior probabilities of all predicted C-terminal readthrough extensions derived from the human transcriptome (see Schueren et al., 2014 for Dataset 1).
evidence: This describes the application of the PTS1 prediction algorithm.

claim: The product of RTP LINiter scores and PTS1 posterior probabilities was used as a predictor of functional peroxisomal targeting by a hidden PTS1 in the extension.
source: Based on the assumption that a protein is more likely to target to peroxisomes by a cryptic PTS1 when the RTP and the extension's PTS1 scores are high, we used the product of RTP LINiter scores and PTS1 posterior probabilities as a predictor of functional peroxisomal targeting by a hidden PTS1 in the extension (see Schueren et al., 2014 for Dataset 1).
evidence: This describes the combined scoring approach.

claim: LDHB was identified at the top (position 1 of 42,069 entries) of the sorted list of combined RTP+ and PTS1 scores.
